doc.title: Jane Bunnett interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, January 25, 2024

title: Visas, first trips to Cuba and founding Spirits of Havana
summary: Bunnett describes decades of visa work, her and Larry's first Cuba trip, discovering Cuban genres and founding Spirits of Havana alongside straight-ahead playing.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Quitting the band: why sidemen left

blocks.x: Yeah it has been, you know, to do all — you know it’s hard enough touring but to do all the extra work that, you know, that we’ve had to do to get people, you know, into Canada, into the U.S. It’s been an ongoing thing for probably forty-something years. I mean our first time, Larry and mine — my partner, trumpet playing producer husband first went to Cuba I guess ’81, ’82 and that’s when we sort of got very, you know, it was a huge surprise going to Cuba and, you know hearing the music that we were hearing and as we continued to keep visiting it was just, we kept discovering more genres of the music and, you know, I’ve always, we’ve always been interested in the history of jazz and then you get into the history of Cuban music and it’s so deep and rich and it’s just a beautiful journey. But then we established our very first group, Spirits of Havana, with a whole bunch of young — not all young people but some older legendary musicians that came through Spirits of Havana that are no longer with us on Earth. But in some ways all that work, it did establish us as doing something a little different than other people were doing in the jazz, on the jazz scene. First of all I consider myself a jazz artist. That’s why I, you know I love the music so much. I love improvising. And I love the history of jazz. And then getting into the Cuban music, you know that’s when we started, as we learned more and more about the genre, to bring our ideas into the many rhythmic concepts and the history of Cuban music. So that’s been that journey. And it’s always sort of gone alongside of some of the other more straight ahead musical endeavors if it was playing with Paul Bley or Don Pullen, Stanley Cowell, Dewey Redman, Billy Hart. © Fillius Jazz Archive -2-
